en.title: Managing AI Agents in CI/CD: Why You Must Enable Stale Approval Dismissal to Prevent Unauthorized Code Merges
en.summary: When using coding agents to generate pull requests, a dangerous race condition often arises: an agent might push an additional commit to fix linting errors or minor bugs after a human has already approved the original PR. This creates a security gap where the final merged code contains changes that were never human-reviewed. To mitigate this, engineering teams must configure GitHub branch protection rules to enable "Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed." This critical setting automatically revokes human approval whenever new code is committed to the branch. By forcing a re-review of the delta, teams ensure that AI agents never bypass the final human quality gate, maintaining strict security and trust in automated workflows.

en.summary: Simon Willison’s 'Quick Study' project demonstrates how Claude 3.5 Opus can generate complex, high-performance web tools directly within an Artifact. By leveraging the Canvas API and a custom Sobel edge detection algorithm, the tool rapidly transforms user-uploaded photos into simulated oil paintings entirely in the browser without relying on external libraries like P5.js or OpenCV. This experiment underscores a critical shift for builders: LLMs are now capable of architecting sophisticated mathematical image-processing logic from scratch, bypassing the need for heavy dependencies. en.summary: Recent investigations into AI-generated history content reveal a pervasive issue: LLMs frequently fabricate events, citing them with authoritative confidence while lacking genuine contextual understanding of causal history. Because these models prioritize probabilistic token prediction over verified factual accuracy, they are prone to producing hallucinations that seem perfectly plausible to general users. Developers building educational or historical applications must stop treating generative output as a primary source of truth. The practical takeaway is to strictly implement RAG architectures that tether AI responses to curated, authoritative historical databases. Without explicit verification layers and attribution mechanisms, building AI tools for historical information remains a high-risk venture that can actively degrade public information ecosystems rather than support them.
